an0921.user: Trying to make sense of my YouTube ads for my apparel label. Last 30 days I got about 47,000 visits to the site, roughly 3,700 added something to cart, around 2,379 actually reached the checkout page, but only 611 bought. CTR on the ads is 2.2%. I keep thinking I need better creatives or more budget to fix the sales but honestly not sure where the problem even is.
an0921.assistant:
Your ads are doing their job — the leak is at the very last step, and you're about to spend money fixing the wrong thing.

Walk the funnel: 3,731 add-to-carts on 47,000 visits is an 8% ATC rate — that's healthy, your traffic and offer are landing. People reach checkout — 2,379 of them. Then it falls off a cliff: only 611 of those 2,379 actually pay. That's a 26% checkout-to-purchase rate, when a working store does 50–70%. So nearly three out of four people who pulled out their wallet walked away at the payment screen.

That is not a creative problem and not a budget problem. Something in your checkout is killing intent at the final click — usually surprise shipping cost revealed late, a forced account login, or no UPI / COD option (huge for Indian buyers). Right now you'd be pouring more ad spend into a bucket that empties at the till.

The one move: go through your own checkout on mobile as a stranger would, and instrument each step in analytics so you can see exactly where the 1,768 lost buyers drop. Fix that screen before you touch the ads.

Caveat — 611 purchases is enough to trust the 26% read, but confirm it isn't one broken payment method by segmenting checkout by UPI vs card vs COD.

an0922.user: Something's gone wrong with my Google Search ads for my jewellery brand and I think the algorithm's turned on me. Six weeks ago my CAC was around ₹499, now it's ₹900. When the same people see the same ad past roughly 2.5 times, they stop clicking. Your sliding CTR is that happening in real time — and because Search/auction pricing makes you pay more for each result as response drops, your CAC nearly doubled, ₹499 to ₹900. Nothing in the targeting changed; the audience just got bored.

Here's why it actually hurts now: contribution is ₹1,700 × 45% − ₹900 = ₹765 − ₹900 = −₹135 per order. Six weeks ago at ₹499 CAC you were making ₹266 a sale; today every order loses you ₹135. The economics flipped, not the algorithm.

The lever is creative refresh — new angles, new hooks, not a colour tweak on the same ad — and build a cadence where you're always testing a fresh challenger so you never ride one winner into the ground again.

One caveat: a 45% margin gives you a thin cushion, so even after the refresh, ₹900 CAC won't be survivable. Refreshing has to pull CAC back toward ₹600 for this to make money — track contribution, not ROAS, as you do it.

an0928.assistant:

A 0.7% conversion rate — 160 orders from nearly 23,000 clicks — means you're filling the top of the funnel with people who are browsing, not buying. That's the signature of broad-match: it matches your ads to loosely-related, low-intent searches, so you pay for clicks from people nowhere near a purchase decision.

So CTR isn't your lever, and neither is the creative. Intent is. You're optimising for clicks when you should be optimising for the right clicks. Broad-match is quietly spending your budget on curiosity.

The move: tighten match types — phrase/exact on your proven buyer terms — and build out a negative-keyword list to choke off the junk queries that are inflating clicks and starving conversions. Optimise the campaign toward conversions, not click volume.

Caveat: pull a search-terms report first and actually read what queries are triggering you — that confirms the intent leak and shows you exactly which negatives to add, rather than guessing. And 160 orders is enough to trust the 0.7% as a real signal, not noise.

an0930.user: Simple question, hopefully. My eyewear YouTube ads — Meta's dashboard says ROAS is 4.1, but my Shopify reports show 1.5 last-click on the same ₹4.5L spend. The two screens flat-out disagree and I genuinely can't tell which one is telling the truth. Which number do I trust?
an0930.assistant:
Neither — because both are lying to you in opposite directions, and the truth is sitting in between.

Meta's 4.1 is inflated: it counts modelled conversions and claims credit on a 7-day-click (often plus view-through) window, so it scoops up sales it merely influenced. Shopify's last-click 1.5 is deflated the other way: it hands all the credit to whatever channel the customer clicked last — usually a branded Google search or a direct visit — and gives YouTube nothing for the discovery it actually drove. So you've set two biased referees against each other, and they will never agree, no matter how long you stare.

Stop refereeing dashboards. The number that doesn't lie is blended CAC: total ad spend across everything ÷ the actual count of new customers in Shopify for that period. On this channel's ₹4.5L, that single figure tells you what you truly paid to acquire a customer — no attribution model required.

The lever: pick blended CAC as your north star, set a target you need to hit for the unit economics to work, and manage spend up or down against that. Let the platform ROAS be a directional signal only.

Caveat: blended CAC blurs which channel did the work, so once it's stable, run the occasional geo or spend-holdout test to see what YouTube specifically is really contributing — that's how you cut through attribution honestly.

The honest answer is: you can't know yet, and neither can I. Eight conversions over seven days is too thin to conclude anything.

The move: let it run untouched to about 100 conversions, or a clean 2–3 week window, whichever comes first. That's the threshold where the CAC stabilises into something you can actually trust and act on.

Until you hit it, the right action is patience — keep it live, don't touch the budget, and resist the urge to judge it early.
